results.title: PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data | alphaXiv
results.content:
Joint generation matters because naive alternatives fail visibly. Figure 8 shows direct video-model calls, either with all cameras on one canvas or with cameras generated separately, producing contradictions with the simulation, such as extra grippers, cups already stacked that should not be, or a cube still on the table that the simulator placed in a drawer. These are pictured examples, not a measured error rate.

Figure 8: direct video generation versus DataFarm on two tasks

Two tasks (stack cups, pull drawer) rendered from the same simulator input. Direct video generation, whether on one canvas or per camera, contradicts the simulation across views; the DataFarm column stays consistent across views and with the simulator. [...] The sharper test is the Sim + DR baseline. It uses the same grounding, expert, and simulated trajectories as DataFarm, but renders observations directly in simulation with domain-randomized textures, lighting, and distractors. In the unseen condition it scores 21 out of 100 versus DataFarm's 87. This points to the observation-production pipeline as important in this experiment, but it does not isolate photographic realism as the sole cause, since the two rendering pipelines differ in more than one respect. The authors attribute the advantage to varying appearance around fixed, exact trajectories.

## One setup, many episodes [...] The closest prior work, CRAFT, also pairs simulator trajectories with edge-conditioned video generation, but starts with a few real teleoperation demonstrations and a digital twin. DataFarm's claimed difference is to build the task from a single calibration episode, reuse none of its actions, and separately review generated episodes before admitting them.

The expert is then developed in a sandboxed harness that is shared by all tasks. The
author writes a controller as a program , requests rollouts on development seeds, and receives the
judge’s verdict on each, but it can neither read the judge nor run the held-out seeds
on which the expert is finally admitted; the harness alone executes rollouts and
records every attempt and its cost. The author may explore
freely during development, for example by trying alternative grasps on development
seeds, but such trials are search rather than demonstrations: an
admitted trajectory must be a single continuous execution, run afresh by the harness,
that passes the judge. Each produced episode samples the task’s object and sensor [...] user never has to supply images that the episode already contains. [...] farm is closer than the simulator on every task (Appendix E).
